Duchi-Hazan-Singer's AdaGrad and McMahan-Streeter's FTPRL were developed concurrently (both 2010-2011) in different communities. Both derive nearly identical regret bounds of the form sum_i D_i sqrt(sum_t g_{t,i}^2) for diagonal adaptive regularization, and both formulate the same regularizer-selection optimization problem (trace-constrained quadratic). Setting $\beta_1 = 0$ in Adam recovers RMSProp's update up to bias correction. Adam additionally supplies an online-convex-optimization regret analysis that is entirely absent from the RMSProp lecture, and bundles AdaMax/temporal-averaging variants. Paper B is a PDF-fallback extraction (math fidelity reduced); names and types were weighted over LaTeX form.

paper_a.title: Mastering the Game of Go with Deep Neural Networks and Tree Search

pairs.why_related: Both papers use the same overarching method: a deep neural network trained by self-play on a two-player perfect-information game, with the network learning to predict the game's expected outcome (value) and being used (directly or via search) for move selection. AlphaGo extends and scales this template (separate policy + value networks, REINFORCE policy gradient and MSE value regression instead of TD($\lambda$), and large-scale MCTS at decision time) to the much harder game of Go. TD-Gammon's TD($\lambda$) self-play training of an MLP value function for backgammon is the methodological ancestor; Silver et al. cite it as the canonical precedent for self-play RL on board games.

paper_a.title: Phase transition of the largest eigenvalue for non-null complex sample covariance matrices

paper_b.title: On the Distribution of the Length of the Longest Increasing Subsequence of Random Permutations

pairs.why_related: Both papers prove Tracy-Widom-type limits for largest-eigenvalue / largest-row-length statistics via Riemann-Hilbert / Fredholm-determinant steepest-descent. Baik-Deift-Johansson (paper B, 1999) establishes the Tracy-Widom $F_{GUE}$ limit for the longest increasing subsequence of a random permutation, anchoring the universality class. BBP (paper A, 2005) extends Tracy-Widom universality to the spiked complex sample-covariance model: it preserves $F_0=F_{GUE}$ in the sub-critical regime and discovers a new family of limit distributions $F_k$ (Airy + finite-rank perturbation) and a Gaussian regime $G_k$ governed by the spike strength. The relation is a clean extension: the same machinery (Fredholm determinant, Airy/PII parametrix, steep-descent contour) now produces a phase transition rather than a single universal law.

paper_a.title: On the Multilinear Restriction and Kakeya conjectures

pairs.why_related: Bennett-Carbery-Tao (paper A) prove the multilinear Kakeya inequality with arbitrarily small $\delta^{-\eps}$ loss at the endpoint exponent $q=d/(d-1)$ via a heat-flow / monotonicity argument generalising Loomis-Whitney. Guth (paper B) closes the endpoint by removing the $\delta^{-\eps}$ loss and obtaining sharp $\theta$-dependence, using an entirely different polynomial-method machinery (polynomial ham sandwich + Lusternik-Schnirelmann visibility). Paper B thus extends paper A's main theorem (Conjecture MLKC / Theorem kakthm) to the sharp endpoint, while overlap of intermediate machinery is minimal: only the underlying objects (transversal $\delta$-tubes / cylinders) and the cited Loomis-Whitney inequality are shared.

Both share the two-stage pre-train/fine-tune framework, the same evaluation suite (GLUE), the same Transformer backbone, and overlapping fine-tuning machinery; BERT explicitly contrasts itself with GPT and reports head-to-head numbers.

paper_a.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption without Bootstrapping

Their relinearisation/key-switching primitives correspond directly (digit-decomposition <-> BitDecomp/Powersof2, modulus-switching relin <-> Scale + SwitchKey). Parallel rediscovery / parallel formulation of the same underlying scheme.

This removes BN's mini-batch dependence and yields identical train/test computation, enabling RNN and small-batch use. pairs.why_related: Black-Scholes (1973) and Merton (1973) are the canonical parallel-rediscovery pair: contemporaneous derivations of the same European option pricing PDE and closed-form formula via different routes. Black-Scholes derive the PDE from a continuously rebalanced riskless hedge under CAPM-style equilibrium, while Merton derives a more general PDE (with stochastic bond price) from a no-arbitrage zero-net-investment portfolio that does NOT require CAPM. Merton additionally develops an extensive no-dominance/no-arbitrage bound theory (Theorems 1-13) that Black-Scholes do not cover, and treats dividends, perpetual American puts, down-and-out calls, and callable warrants. The shared core (PDE, closed-form formula, put-call parity, no-early-exercise of American calls) aligns tightly; Merton's broader theory is paper-specific.

The papers are parallel rediscoveries of the PRG-from-hardness paradigm, with Yao providing the abstract framework and BBS the concrete number-theoretic instantiation.

paper_a.title: Decoding by Linear Programming

paper_b.title: Simultaneous Analysis of Lasso and Dantzig Selector

Candes-Tao formulate the Restricted Isometry Property (delta_S) plus restricted orthogonality (theta_{S,S'}) and prove exact-recovery / robust-recovery theorems under delta_S + theta_S + theta_{S,2S} < 1. Bickel-Ritov-Tsybakov instead introduce the weaker Restricted Eigenvalue (RE) assumption tailored to noisy regression and establish prediction / coefficient oracle inequalities for both estimators simultaneously, reducing classical RIP-type conditions (now phi_min versus theta_{m_1,m_2}) to sufficient conditions for RE. The pair is paradigmatic competing frameworks: same underlying problem (L1-recovery of sparse signals from linear observations) attacked with different design-matrix conditions and different proof machinery.

paper_b.title: Compressed Sensing

Candes-Tao (paper A) builds a Restricted Isometry Property / Restricted Orthogonality framework around constants $\delta_S, \theta_{S,S'}$ and proves exact $\ell_1$ recovery of S-sparse signals via dual-certificate construction. Donoho (paper B) builds a Gel'fand-width / CS1-CS3 framework controlling nullspace concentration $\nu(\Phi,J)$ and proves near-optimal $\ell_2$ approximation rates of compressible signals. The two papers tackle the same underlying problem (sparse recovery via $\ell_1$ minimization with random Gaussian / spherical sampling) using genuinely disjoint technical vocabularies; matches are mostly at the level of conceptual roles rather than exact mathematical objects, justifying the CF (competing frameworks) classification.

paper_a.title: Sampling Signals with Finite Rate of Innovation

paper_b.title: Compressed Sensing

pairs.why_related: Both papers prove that signals with structured low-dimensional content can be recovered from far fewer linear measurements than the ambient (Nyquist / pixel) rate, but they are independent rediscoveries from different communities. Vetterli-Marziliano-Blu's FRI route is deterministic and parametric: model the signal as a finite stream of Diracs / splines / piecewise polynomials, sample via a sinc / Gaussian / spline kernel, and recover via the annihilating-filter method (Yule-Walker, root finding, Vandermonde solve) at exactly the rate of innovation rho. Donoho's CS route is probabilistic and geometric: model the signal as having transform coefficients in an ell_p ball, take a random linear projection (a CS / RIP-style matrix), and recover via convex ell_1 minimization at rate (n/log N)^{-r}. Both papers obtain sub-Nyquist exact / near-optimal recovery but from disjoint machinery (Toeplitz-Vandermonde algebra vs Gel'fand-width / spherical-section probability), with no formal cross-reference: a textbook parallel-rediscovery pair.

Gowers proves a fully quantitative version of Szemeredi's theorem covering all $k$, which strictly extends every density question raised in the 1936 paper, via higher-order Fourier analysis (Gowers norms) — a wholly new technical apparatus far beyond the elementary case-analysis used in 1936. This is a textbook EXT relationship: same fundamental object, generalized to all $k$ with explicit (tower-type) bounds. Almost every Perelman node has a near-verbatim counterpart in Kleiner-Lott, while Kleiner-Lott has a substantial body of paper-original surgery/geometrization material with no Perelman-paper-1 counterpart (because that material lives in Perelman's papers II and III, which are not part of this pair).

paper_a.title: Learning from Delayed Rewards (PhD thesis)

paper_b.title: On-Line Q-Learning Using Connectionist Systems

pairs.why_related: Watkins (1989) introduces one-step Q-learning, an off-policy TD method that bootstraps from $\max_b Q(x_{t+1},b)$, together with the Action-Replay-Process convergence proof for the lookup-table case and a TD($\lambda$) extension whose convergence remained open. Rummery & Niranjan (1994) propose Modified Connectionist Q-Learning (MCQ-L, later renamed SARSA), an on-policy alternative that bootstraps from $Q(x_{t+1}, a_{t+1})$ for the action actually selected. The two papers tackle the same RL action-value-estimation problem with the same TD($\lambda$)/eligibility-trace machinery but with substantially different update targets and theoretical properties (off-policy vs on-policy, convergence proven for tabular Q-learning vs no proof for the connectionist on-policy variant), making this a competing-frameworks pair.

paper_a.title: Random Forests

paper_b.title: Bagging Predictors

pairs.why_related: Random Forests (Breiman 2001) extends Bagging Predictors (Breiman 1996, originally 1994 TR-421) by injecting an additional source of randomness--random feature subset selection at each tree split--on top of the bootstrap-aggregating skeleton. Paper A explicitly cites bagging as a building block (AP268.6 origin=external; AP268.1 'specializes' bagging), reuses bootstrap sampling and majority voting, and develops a new strength/correlation theory (TP268.2, TP268.4) that supersedes bagging's variance-reduction argument (TP269.1) by tracking the c/s^2 ratio rather than learning-set variance. Both papers are PDF-fallback so confidence is downgraded where LaTeX would have disambiguated.

paper_a.title: Boosting Algorithms as Gradient Descent

paper_b.title: A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting

pairs.why_related: Mason et al. (paper277) recast AdaBoost (paper270) as a special case of AnyBoost, a generic functional gradient-descent procedure on convex combinations of base hypotheses. The same AdaBoost algorithm is re-derived as coordinate descent on the exponential margin loss in function space, providing an alternative interpretation and proof technique (gradient descent / convergence in function space) for the original Freund-Schapire result. The pair fits the AP (alternative proof) relation: same algorithmic object, fundamentally different theoretical machinery (functional gradient vs. multiplicative-weights potential).

paper_a.title: Regret-based continuous-time dynamics (Hart & Mas-Colell 2003)

paper_b.title: A Short Introduction to Boosting (Freund & Schapire 1999)

pairs.why_related: Both papers describe iterative multiplicative-style updates that achieve no-regret/exponentially-vanishing-error guarantees: paper A (Hart-Mas-Colell) is the game-theoretic regret-matching/regret-based dynamics line, while paper B (Freund-Schapire) is the boosting/AdaBoost line. AdaBoost's exponential reweighting on misclassified examples and Hart-Mas-Colell's gradient-of-potential reweighting on positive-regret actions are parallel rediscoveries of the multiplicative-weights / no-regret idea in distinct communities (machine learning vs game theory); paper B explicitly notes the game-theoretic interpretation in remark RP279.3. Note: both extractions are PDF-fallbacks with reduced math fidelity, and both have registry-mismatch notes; the alignment is based on the ACTUAL PDF contents.

paper_a.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

paper_b.title: Highway Networks

pairs.why_related: Both papers attack the same problem (training very deep feedforward networks) by inserting a parallel input-side path around stacked nonlinear layers, but with substantially different machinery: Highway uses learned data-dependent transform/carry gates (LSTM-inspired) so a layer interpolates between identity and H(x), while ResNet drops the gating entirely and adds an unconditional identity shortcut, learning only the residual F(x) = H(x) - x. The two are structurally siblings (Highway's T -> 0 limit is exactly ResNet's identity-shortcut block with F replaced by H), but their theoretical framing, parameter cost, and empirical regimes differ enough that we classify them as competing frameworks rather than one extending the other.

paper_a.title: A statistical model for tensor PCA

paper_b.title: Statistical limits of spiked tensor models

pairs.why_related: Both papers study the spiked tensor model T = lambda x^{otimes d} + W. Richard-Montanari (paper A) introduce the model and analyze it from an algorithmic / statistical-physics angle: ML upper bounds, tensor unfolding, power iteration, AMP with state evolution, PSD-cone-constrained projection, plus a Fano-style information-theoretic lower bound. Perry-Wein-Bandeira (paper B) extend the same model to a sharper statistical-decision-theoretic analysis: they derive matching contiguity-based detection/recovery lower bounds for general priors via a noise-conditioned second-moment method, treat spherical / Rademacher / sparse-Rademacher priors uniformly, and tighten the spherical upper bound below mu_d using a BBP eigenvalue argument. The relationship is best classified as EXT: B inherits A's setup and ABC noise-norm result, then extends to an optimal information-theoretic theory across multiple priors.

paper_a.title: On Some Sequences of Integers

paper_b.title: On Some Sequences of Integers

pairs.why_related: REGISTRY DATA ERROR: This pair was curated to compare Roth (1953) 'On Certain Sets of Integers' (paper342) against Behrend (1946) 'On Sets of Integers Which Contain No Three Terms in Arithmetical Progression' (paper341), with hypothesised relation CF (Behrend's lower bound construction vs Roth's matching upper bound). Both extractions document this registry mismatch in metadata.registry_mismatch_note. Comparing a paper to itself does not yield a meaningful Roth-vs-Behrend alignment, so we mark NEG. The two extractions are essentially the same content (definitions of A-sequence and r(N), Theorem I r(2N) <= N+1 (or N) for N>=8, Theorem II density bound near 3/8 or 1/2, the same proofs by induction with reflection/translation/subadditivity, the same base cases r(8)=4 .. r(14)=8 and r(17)=8, the same r(41)=16 witness, the same Szekeres conjecture and ternary construction). Match entries below pair the trivially-corresponding nodes for completeness, but the pair itself contributes no signal about Roth vs Behrend; the underlying source data needs to be re-fetched.

paper_a.title: SAGA: A Fast Incremental Gradient Method With Support for Non-Strongly Convex Composite Objectives

paper_b.title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient Descent using Predictive Variance Reduction

pairs.why_related: SAGA (paper A) directly extends SVRG (paper B) and SAG within a shared variance-reduction template $\theta_\alpha = \alpha(X-Y) + \mathbb{E}Y$. SAGA replaces SVRG's snapshot $\tilde{x}$ (refreshed only between outer epochs) with a per-sample stored gradient table updated at every step, retaining unbiasedness ($\alpha=1$, unlike SAG's biased $\alpha=1/n$) while removing the two-loop epoch structure. SAGA additionally adds support for proximal/composite objectives and a non-strongly-convex $O(n/k)$ rate not in the original SVRG paper. The proof of SAGA's Theorem 1 reuses the SVRG-style $\|a+b\|^2 \leq (1+\beta^{-1})\|a\|^2 + (1+\beta)\|b\|^2$ variance argument and the same per-component smoothness inequality (Lemma 2 here = SVRG's Eq. (8)).

paper_a.title: Exact Recovery in the Stochastic Block Model

paper_b.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

pairs.why_related: Stochastic Block Model exact-recovery (Abbe-Bandeira-Hall, sparse random-graph community detection, sharp information-theoretic threshold via ML / SDP / Matrix Bernstein) vs Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho-Jain-Abbeel, continuous-state Gaussian Markov-chain generative model trained by a variational ELBO and a noise-prediction MSE). The two papers share at most the abstract notion 'stochastic model'. Their objects (sparse 2-block random graph vs Gaussian diffusion latent-variable model), their target tasks (combinatorial community recovery vs image generation / density modelling), their proof techniques (binomial-difference tail bounds, Matrix Bernstein, KKT/SDP duality vs ELBO derivations, Gaussian-KL Rao-Blackwellisation, reparameterisation tricks), and their algorithms (ML / SDP / partial-recovery+local-flip vs SGD training of a noise predictor and ancestral Langevin-like sampling) have no meaningful node-level correspondence. No exact or analogous matches were found after honest inspection.

paper_a.title: Robust Stochastic Approximation Approach to Stochastic Programming

paper_b.title: Stochastic First- and Zeroth-order Methods for Nonconvex Stochastic Programming

pairs.why_related: Ghadimi-Lan (paper B) extends the classical/robust SA framework of Nemirovski-Juditsky-Lan-Shapiro (paper A) from the convex setting to nonconvex smooth stochastic optimization. The key extension: paper A obtains O(1/sqrt(N)) rates on the optimality gap E[f(x_avg)-f*] under convexity using projection/mirror-descent and iterate averaging, while paper B obtains analogous O(1/sqrt(N)) rates on the expected squared gradient norm E||grad f(x_R)||^2 by using a randomly-indexed iterate (RSG) instead of averaging, and further extends the framework to derivative-free (zeroth-order) settings via Gaussian smoothing. Both papers share the Juditsky-Nemirovski martingale large-deviation lemma and parallel two-phase / averaging meta-strategies for high-probability bounds.

paper_a.title: Making Gradient Descent Optimal for Strongly Convex Stochastic Optimization

paper_b.title: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling

pairs.why_related: Paper A analyses convergence rates of stochastic gradient descent for strongly convex stochastic optimization (last-iterate, average, suffix-average; upper and lower bounds of order 1/T or log T/T). Paper B introduces Flow Matching, a simulation-free regression objective for training continuous normalizing flows by matching a neural vector field to a (conditional) target vector field that generates a probability density path. Despite both involving gradients in some surface sense (SGD updates vs gradient of a regression loss in CNF training), the problems, mathematical objects (convex functions on R^d under noisy subgradient oracles vs probability density paths and time-dependent vector fields under the continuity equation), techniques (martingale concentration, projection inequalities, induction on 1/t recurrences vs Leibniz rule for the marginal-VF identity, OT/diffusion path constructions), and theorems are entirely disjoint. No paper-A node aligns with any paper-B node beyond a shared but uninformative use of generic gradient/stochastic-sampling vocabulary.

paper_a.title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient Descent using Predictive Variance Reduction

paper_b.title: A Stochastic Gradient Method with an Exponential Convergence Rate for Finite Training Sets

pairs.why_related: Two competing variance-reduction frameworks for the same finite-sum smooth strongly-convex optimization problem. Both achieve linear convergence at the cost of one full-data pass per amortized stage. SAG (paper B) keeps a per-sample memory of the most recent gradient and forms a biased running average; SVRG (paper A) periodically refreshes a full-gradient snapshot and uses an unbiased control-variate update. The proof techniques differ substantially: SVRG analyses smoothness/control-variate algebra summed over an inner loop, while SAG constructs a quadratic Lyapunov function on an enlarged state vector.

paper_a.title: Boosting the Margin: A New Explanation for the Effectiveness of Voting Methods

paper_b.title: Empirical Margin Distributions and Bounding the Generalization Error of Combined Classifiers

pairs.why_related: Both papers establish margin-based generalization bounds for voting/boosting classifiers, but via fundamentally different proof machinery. Schapire-Freund-Bartlett-Lee (1998) prove the foundational bound P_D[yf(x)<=0] <= P_S[yf(x)<=theta] + O(m^{-1/2} (log|H| / theta^2 + log(1/delta))^{1/2}) (and its VC-dimension variant) via a probabilistic construction of an N-element 'sloppy cover' C_N of the convex hull C, decomposing the margin event through C_N, then Chernoff + union bound (or Devroye/Sauer for the VC version) and optimizing N ~ theta^{-2} log(m|H|/delta). Koltchinskii-Panchenko (2002) re-prove and substantially refine the same theorem -- and extend it to a whole family of margin-cost-function bounds, multiclass, neural networks and oracle inequalities -- via Rademacher/Gaussian complexity and empirical-process theory (martingale/bounded-difference concentration, Ledoux-Talagrand contraction, Slepian's lemma, Talagrand concentration). The Schapire et al. convex-hull boosting bound (TP115.1/TP115.2) is the special case TP116.12 of the KP framework -- KP explicitly state Theorem 12 'improves Schapire et al. (1998) margin bound for boosting on VC base classes'. Both papers are PDF-fallback extractions, so trust names/types over exact LaTeX. The pair is best classified as AP (alternative proof) with a strong EXT flavor (KP go far beyond Schapire et al.'s setting).

paper_a.title: Cardinal arithmetic for skeptics

paper_b.title: Mice with finitely many Woodin cardinals from optimal determinacy hypotheses

pairs.why_related: Two set-theoretic foundational programs operating on disjoint corners of the subject. Shelah develops PCF / pseudopower theory to bound singular cardinal arithmetic in ZFC alone (no large-cardinal hypotheses); Muller-Schindler-Woodin work in inner-model theory, deriving the existence and iterability of mice with finitely many Woodin cardinals from optimal projective determinacy hypotheses. Both papers share the broad set-theoretic vocabulary (cardinals, cofinality, ultrafilters/iteration, large cardinals) but their main objects (pcf, pp, covering numbers vs $M_n^\#$, Q-structures, iteration trees, projective determinacy) are non-overlapping research programs aimed at different parts of the universe of sets. Almost every paper-original Level-1 contribution on each side has no counterpart on the other; the only contentful cross-paper matches are in the shared classical background (cofinality, large cardinals as obstructions/hypotheses).

paper_a.title: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

paper_b.arxiv_id: Bernstein-Vazirani 1997 (registry mismatch: paper318 is actually Bernstein-Vazirani 'Quantum complexity theory' SIAM J. Comput., not Simon 1994)
paper_b.title: Quantum complexity theory

pairs.why_related: Shor's paper (paper_a) extends the quantum-algorithmic Fourier-sampling framework that Bernstein-Vazirani (paper_b) develop to factoring and discrete logarithm. Paper_b builds the QTM model, the universal QTM, the BQP definition, the Hadamard/Fourier-sampling primitive, and proves its 'recursive Fourier sampling' oracle separation; paper_a uses essentially the same QFT-based interference idea with a non-binary modulus q to extract periods from group elements. The papers are therefore in an EXT relationship: paper_a applies and generalises paper_b's Fourier-sampling technique (with QFT mod q replacing the Hadamard $\bmod 2$ transform). Note: paper318 is Bernstein-Vazirani, not Simon as the pair name suggests; alignment is performed on actual contents.

paper_a.title: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations

paper_b.title: Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning

pairs.why_related: SimCLR and MoCo are competing frameworks for unsupervised visual representation learning by contrastive (InfoNCE-style) losses on two augmented views of an image. They share the same problem, the same loss family, the instance-discrimination pretext task, and a closely related encoder-then-similarity training loop, but differ fundamentally in how negatives are supplied: SimCLR enlarges the in-batch dictionary (very large minibatches with symmetric in-batch negatives, plus an MLP projection head and aggressive augmentations), while MoCo decouples dictionary size from batch size via a FIFO queue of past keys whose encoder is a momentum moving average of the query encoder. Almost every conceptual node in one paper has a counterpart in the other, but several MoCo-specific contributions (queue, momentum encoder, shuffling BN) and SimCLR-specific contributions (NT-Xent symmetric loss, projection head, color-augmentation emphasis, LARS large-batch tricks) have no analogue.

paper_a.title: Spectral Sparsification of Graphs

paper_b.title: Twice-Ramanujan Sparsifiers

pairs.why_related: Both papers solve the spectral graph sparsification problem. Spielman-Teng (paper 117) gives a randomized nearly-linear-time algorithm producing (1+epsilon)-sparsifiers with O(n log^c n / epsilon^2) edges via edge-sampling on high-conductance pieces of a graph decomposition. Batson-Spielman-Srivastava (paper 118, 'Twice-Ramanujan') extends the result by a fundamentally different deterministic barrier-method potential argument, achieving the optimal O(n) edge count at near-Ramanujan condition number — at the cost of polynomial running time and randomization. Paper 117 itself cites BSS in its final remarks as the subsequent improvement. The relation is EXT: BSS strengthens the edge-count bound and removes randomization while sharing the underlying spectral-approximation problem and Laplacian quadratic-form formulation.

paper_a.title: A Differential Equation for Modeling Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method: Theory and Insights

paper_b.title: Some Methods of Speeding Up the Convergence of Iteration Methods

pairs.why_related: Su-Boyd-Candes (2014) extends Polyak's (1964) heavy-ball framework: Polyak introduced both the discrete two-step momentum iteration $x^{n+1}=x^n-\alpha P(x^n)+\beta(x^n-x^{n-1})$ and its continuous analogue $\ddot x = \alpha_2 \dot x + \alpha_1 P(x)$, proved local convergence with rate $(\sqrt M-\sqrt m)/(\sqrt M+\sqrt m)$ for strongly convex quadratics, and developed a general $k$-step iteration / $k$-th order ODE theory. Su-Boyd-Candes derive the time-varying-damping ODE $\ddot X+(3/t)\dot X+\nabla f(X)=0$ as the continuous limit of Nesterov's accelerated method, establish $O(1/t^2)$ on convex (not just strongly convex) $f$ via a Lyapunov energy, generalize to damping $r/t$, and extend to composite/non-smooth and strongly-convex regimes with restarting. The two papers thus instantiate the same conceptual programme — second-order momentum ODEs as a tool for analysing accelerated first-order methods — with Su-Boyd-Candes deepening it for the Nesterov branch. Paper B is PDF-fallback (1964 classic), so node names/types are weighted over LaTeX fidelity.

paper_a.title: Attention Is All You Need

paper_b.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

pairs.why_related: Bahdanau et al. (2015) introduced soft additive attention over BiRNN encoder annotations as an add-on to an RNN encoder-decoder for machine translation. Vaswani et al. (2017) extend this idea by (i) replacing additive attention with a scaled dot-product variant computed in matrix form and stacked into multi-head blocks, (ii) discarding the recurrence entirely so that attention is the sole mechanism for both source-side encoding and target-side decoding (self-attention in addition to encoder-decoder attention), and (iii) adding sinusoidal positional encodings to recover the order information that the BiRNN previously supplied. The Transformer thus generalises Bahdanau's per-step attention from one cross-attention layer attached to an RNN into a full attention-only sequence transduction architecture; the relationship is best characterised as EXT.

paper_a.title: Greed is Good: Algorithmic Results for Sparse Approximation

paper_b.title: Decoding by Linear Programming

pairs.why_related: Both papers attack the same underlying problem of recovering a sparse vector from an underdetermined linear system, but through substantially different theoretical machinery. Tropp analyzes a greedy algorithm (OMP) alongside Basis Pursuit using a deterministic coherence-based framework (Exact Recovery Condition, cumulative coherence) over a fixed dictionary, while Candes-Tao analyze the convex Basis Pursuit decoder for random Gaussian coding matrices via the Restricted Isometry Property and a dual-certificate construction. The two papers reach overlapping conclusions about exact ell_1 recovery from different angles, qualifying as competing frameworks (CF) for the same recovery question.

paper_a.title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

paper_b.title: Stochastic Backpropagation and Approximate Inference in Deep Generative Models

pairs.why_related: Two essentially simultaneous (2014) and independent derivations of amortised stochastic variational inference for deep continuous-latent directed generative models. Both papers introduce a recognition network jointly trained with the generator, derive a reparameterised low-variance gradient estimator of the variational lower bound (Kingma-Welling: SGVB / 'reparameterization trick'; Rezende et al.: stochastic backpropagation via Bonnet/Price or location-scale reparameterisation), give the closed-form Gaussian KL, and demonstrate the resulting algorithm (AEVB / DLGM learning) on image benchmarks. The Rezende et al. paper additionally develops a hierarchical Gaussian latent model, a structured low-rank covariance, and a missing-data imputation Markov chain; the Kingma-Welling paper additionally treats fully Bayesian parameter inference and an importance-weighted marginal-likelihood estimator. The shared core makes this a textbook example of parallel rediscovery (PR).

paper_a.title: The sphere packing problem in dimension 8

paper_b.title: The sphere packing problem in dimension 24

pairs.why_related: Paper B (Cohn-Kumar-Miller-Radchenko-Viazovska, d=24) directly extends paper A (Viazovska, d=8) by transporting the modular-form magic-function construction from the E8 lattice to the Leech lattice. The two proofs share a near-identical skeleton: Cohn-Elkies LP bound, +1 and -1 radial Fourier eigenfunctions a(r), b(r) built as contour integrals against (quasi)modular forms, contour-deformation/double-zero arguments, and a final A(t)<0 / B(t)>0 verification. Paper B replaces auxiliary forms (φ_{-2}, φ_{-4}, h, ψ_I) by a quasimodular weight-(-8) form φ and a weight-(-10) modular form ψ_I for Γ(2), and replaces interval-arithmetic with Sturm-on-truncated-q-series in PARI/GP.

paper_a.title: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm

paper_b.title: Probabilistic Counting Algorithms for Data Base Applications

pairs.why_related: HyperLogLog (Flajolet-Fusy-Gandouet-Meunier 2007) is a direct refinement/extension of Flajolet-Martin's Probabilistic Counting with Stochastic Averaging (PCSA, 1985). Both solve streaming cardinality estimation via bit-pattern observables of hashed values combined with stochastic averaging across m substreams; both rely on Mellin-transform / depoissonization asymptotics. HLL replaces FM's leftmost-zero-of-BITMAP observable (R) with the per-substream maximum leftmost-1-position (Max), and replaces direct averaging by the harmonic mean, trading FM's 0.78/sqrt(m) accuracy with 32-bit-per-register storage for HLL's 1.04/sqrt(m) accuracy at log_2 log_2 N bits per register. HLL explicitly cites FM as prior work (AP313.4) and inherits its analytical machinery.

paper_a.title: Distribution of Eigenvalues for Some Sets of Random Matrices (Marchenko & Pastur, 1967)

paper_b.title: Characteristic Vectors of Bordered Matrices With Infinite Dimensions (Wigner, 1955)

pairs.why_related: Marchenko-Pastur (paper A, 1967) extends Wigner's semicircle setting (paper B, 1955) to a much broader ensemble: a deterministic self-adjoint operator $A_N$ perturbed by an arbitrary number of i.i.d. rank-one operators $\tau_i (\cdot, q^{(i)}) q^{(i)}$, governed by a concentration $c = \lim n/N$ and a coefficient distribution $\sigma(\tau)$. Where Wigner derives the semicircle density via the combinatorial moment method (Catalan path counts), MP derives a fixed-point integral / Stieltjes-transform equation whose solution is unique. The classical semicircle reappears as the $c \to \infty$ limit of MP's canonical example (ExP321.1, RP321.1), and MP explicitly cites Wigner's 1958 semicircle as TP321.4. Both papers are PDF-fallback extractions, so we lean on `name`/`type` over exact LaTeX. The relationship is best described as EXT (MP generalizes the semicircle setup); SM (same method) does NOT fit because the two derivations use different machinery (Stieltjes transform fixed point vs. moment method).

paper_a.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

paper_b.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation

pairs.why_related: Both papers learn dense word embeddings that encode linear semantic and syntactic regularities (the 'king - man + woman = queen' property), but via competing frameworks. word2vec (paper A) is a local-context, on-line, log-linear neural predictor (CBOW / Skip-gram) that performs implicit factorization of a shifted PMI matrix; GloVe (paper B) is a global, weighted least-squares explicit factorization of the log word-word co-occurrence matrix. They share the analogy task, the cosine-arithmetic solver, AdaGrad optimization and (cited) skip-gram baselines, but diverge sharply on objective, training signal (predict-vs-fit) and complexity analysis (hidden-layer cost vs harmonic-number / power-law).

paper_a.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System

paper_b.title: Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine

pairs.why_related: XGBoost (Chen-Guestrin 2016) extends Friedman's Gradient Boosting Machine (1999/2001) along the gradient-boosting skeleton: same additive tree expansion and stagewise greedy fitting, but with explicit L1/L2-style regularization (gamma T + lambda |w|^2), a second-order Taylor approximation that uses Hessian information h_i in addition to the gradient g_i, a closed-form structure score and split gain derived from this approximation, a weighted-quantile sketch with proven approximation guarantees for distributed approximate split finding, a sparsity-aware split algorithm with default directions, and engineering contributions (column blocks, cache-aware access, out-of-core blocks). Friedman's paper provides the conceptual scaffolding (function-space steepest descent, generic Gradient Boost, LS/LAD/M/L2/LK TreeBoost specializations) that XGBoost's more general regularized objective subsumes. Note paper B is PDF-fallback (reduced math fidelity).

paper_a.title: On Model Selection Consistency of Lasso

paper_b.title: High-Dimensional Graphs and Variable Selection with the Lasso

pairs.why_related: Both papers (published essentially in parallel in 2006) establish Lasso support-recovery consistency under an irrepresentable-type condition, but from substantially different angles. Zhao-Yu treat a single sparse linear regression and isolate the Strong/Weak Irrepresentable Condition on the Gram matrix as the (almost) sufficient and necessary requirement for sign consistency, including a fixed-p classical regime and high-dimensional moment/Gaussian regimes. Meinshausen-Buhlmann attack covariance selection in Gaussian graphical models by running per-node Lasso (neighborhood selection); their Assumption 6 (Neighborhood Stability via the signed quantity S_a(b)) is the same population irrepresentable-type condition rephrased through best-linear-prediction coefficients, and they obtain analogous exponential-rate type-I/type-II/edge-set consistency. The relationship is best classified as competing frameworks (CF) on the same underlying support-recovery problem rather than direct rediscovery, since the two papers solve different statistical problems with parallel theory and the M-B paper additionally addresses graph-level aggregation and an oracle-prediction inconsistency that have no Zhao-Yu counterpart.

paper_a.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck-Cesa-Bianchi 2012)

paper_b.title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (Kingma-Welling 2013)

pairs.why_related: Paper A is a survey/monograph on multi-armed bandits and online learning, centred on regret minimization for sequential decision problems (UCB, Exp3/Exp3.P/Exp4, Online Mirror Descent, contextual / linear / nonlinear bandits, semi-bandit, two-/one-point feedback, unimodal stochastic bandits). Paper B introduces the Variational Auto-Encoder: a generative latent-variable model trained by stochastic gradient ascent on a reparameterized variational lower bound (ELBO). The two papers share no mathematical objects, problem statements, theorems, or algorithmic ideas: bandits operate on a discrete or continuous arm/action space with adversarial or stochastic loss feedback and minimize regret w.r.t. a best fixed comparator; VAEs perform amortized approximate posterior inference for a directed latent variable model and minimize a KL-regularized reconstruction objective. Even at the level of broad machinery there is no overlap (concentration / change-of-measure / Bregman-divergence regret bounds vs. change-of-variables / reparameterization for differentiable Monte Carlo expectations). The only superficial commonalities are generic stochastic-gradient style optimization and Monte Carlo expectations, which do not constitute a meaningful structural alignment. All paper-origin Level-1 nodes on each side are emitted as `none`.

paper_a.title: Are Transformers universal approximators of sequence-to-sequence functions?

paper_b.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification

pairs.why_related: These two papers cover essentially disjoint subfields of machine learning. Paper A (Yun et al.) is a pure approximation-theory result on neural-network architecture: fixed-width Transformers with hardmax attention can approximate any continuous permutation-equivariant sequence-to-sequence function in $L^p$. Paper B (Angelopoulos & Bates) is a distribution-free uncertainty-quantification tutorial: split conformal prediction calibrates a black-box model so that its prediction set covers $Y_{\rm test}$ with probability $\geq 1-\alpha$ under exchangeability. There is no shared theorem, no shared object, no shared proof technique; the only conceptual contact point is that both papers exploit a symmetry assumption (permutation equivariance of the Transformer block versus exchangeability of i.i.d. data), but at completely different levels of the stack. Almost every paper-origin Level-1 node has no counterpart on the other side.

paper_a.title: Communication-Efficient Algorithms for Statistical Optimization

paper_b.title: Beyond Locality-Sensitive Hashing

Paper006 (Zhang-Duchi-Wainwright 2013) studies communication-efficient distributed M-estimation via averaging methods (AVGM, SAVGM, SGDAVGM); the contributions are statistical risk bounds of the form $\sigma^2/(nm) + O(n^{-2})$ for averaged local empirical minimizers under smoothness/strong-convexity, plus bias-corrected and SGD variants.
